title: 1 Year in a 2D Browser MMORPG with AI: Real Stack, Model Tiers, Procedural Canvas "Art"
author: BrasilianPianistBoi
selftext:
I've spent the past year building Kapi Online, a retro 2D browser MMORPG running on HTML5 Canvas, Node.js WebSockets, and MongoDB, hosted on two Oracle Cloud free-tier instances.  


A lot of advice about AI game dev reads like LinkedIn hype. As a student working on a budget, here is what actually held up across a year in production.

# What the models were actually good for

* **Google frontier flash models:** They are rougher on edge-case logic than top models, but the pricing and free quotas made them the only realistic option for cheap production.
* **Claude Sonnet 5.5:** The standard for quick refactors and safe edits. It makes surgical changes without rewriting unrelated code or inventing scope.
* **Claude Opus: 5.5** Reserved for high-stakes architecture decisions, WebSocket state sync, and security sanity checks.
* **Sol 6.1:** Useful for extending systems where the rules and boundaries were already written.
* **Argon:** Expensive and ineffective for fast iteration.

# Pure JavaScript Canvas drawing vs. "AI slop"

I skipped sprite sheets. SVGs worked fine for static icons, and Gemini made decent vector shapes, but LLMs struggle to composite dynamic visual assets in canvas code.

Every character, gear layer, and animation in the game is drawn directly with procedural JavaScript Canvas commands. It raises an interesting question: does procedural canvas rendering count as "AI art slop" when almost nobody drew characters in pure JavaScript canvas before LLMs existed? It feels like a distinct workflow altogether.

# Prompt engineering didn't matter much

Long system prompts with complex roleplay instructions usually got in the way. They overcomplicated simple tasks and caused the model to hallucinate constraints.

What worked consistently:

1. Short, narrow context (only the file or function being modified).
2. Explicit constraints on what *not* to touch.
3. Automated unit tests in Jest to catch the regressions that inevitably happen when an LLM edits a live game loop.

# Where the project is now

The game runs in a browser tab with 1-click guest access and no downloads:

[https://mmorpg.kich.dev.br/](https://mmorpg.kich.dev.br/)

It currently has five weapon classes, mounts, an auction house, directional combat with dodge frames, and a 50-player cap per instance across two free-tier servers.

I'm looking for collaborators who want to help ith:

* Art direction and visual cohesion across the canvas elements and UI.
* Balancing combat pacing and the active vs. idle progression loop.

If you test the combat or want to talk, let me know what you think. In the video, a newly added bard class.
